title: ACGME Compliant Residency Schedules Without New Software
description: What the ACGME work hour rules require of a residency schedule, why spreadsheets miss pattern violations, and how programs hand the build to a service.
content:
Summary

  • Every program schedules differently. Some of the rules come from the ACGME. Most do not: which attendings cover which weeks, who cannot be on call the same night as someone else, the rotation one subspecialty will not move, the requests people put in months ago.
  • Fitting all of it together at once is the hard part, and it is why building a schedule by hand takes weeks and why spreadsheets miss the pattern violations.
  • Scheduling Wizard is a managed service: a team that builds physician schedules and nothing else. You send us your rules and requests; we send back the finished schedules. There is no software for your team to learn.

You have inherited the job of building your program's block, call and clinic schedules. If you are an incoming chief resident, or a program director who has taken this on, that means collecting everyone's requests, working out coverage, and fitting rules that mostly are not written down anywhere. Most programs we talk to are piecing all of it together by hand. It takes weeks, and next year a new chief starts over.

Here is what the rules require, and then how programs hand the build off.

What ACGME Compliance Actually Requires: The Six Core Rules

Six ACGME rules shape almost every residency schedule, and a schedule has to meet them at the same time as everything else your program wants. That is what makes building one by hand slow.

1. The 80-Hour Weekly Limit (Averaged Over 4 Weeks)

Residents cannot work more than 80 hours per week, averaged across a rolling 4-week period. Averaging smooths over a heavy week, but a vacation week does not pull it down: the ACGME leaves vacation out of the average, so three heavy weeks are averaged over three weeks.

2. The 24-Hour Continuous Duty Limit

Residents are capped at 24 consecutive hours of clinical and educational work, with up to 4 additional hours permitted for patient safety transitions like handoffs. No new clinical responsibilities can be assigned during those final 4 hours.

3. Required Days Off

At least one full, uninterrupted 24-hour day off per week, averaged over 4 weeks. A common misunderstanding: a "post-call" day does not automatically qualify. The day must be completely free from all clinical and educational obligations.

4. Minimum Rest Between Shifts

Residents should have eight hours off between scheduled clinical work periods, and must have at least 14 hours free after 24 hours of in-house call. A required morning conference the day after a 24-hour call is a common way to cut into those 14 hours without anyone noticing.

5. In-House Call Frequency

In-house call must be scheduled no more frequently than every third night, averaged over 4 weeks. At-home call is not subject to that limit, but clinical work done on at-home call counts toward the 80 hours, and at-home call cannot fall on a resident's free day.

6. PGY-1 Resident Limits, Now Following 24+4

Since 2017, PGY-1 residents follow the same 24+4 rule as all other residents: up to 24 continuous hours of clinical work with up to 4 additional hours for transitions of care and education. Previously, PGY-1s were capped at 16 continuous hours. Programs should make sure their schedule templates reflect the current 24+4 standard for all PGY levels.

Subspecialty-Specific Overlays

These six rules are just the foundation. Each specialty's Review Committee adds its own requirements on top. Surgery programs have case and coverage requirements, family medicine programs have continuity clinic requirements, and other specialties have rules of their own. These specialty rules are often where a hand-built schedule slips, because they sit in a different document from the duty hour rules.

Where Schedules and Hour Tracking Miss ACGME Violations

Spreadsheets are fine for laying out a schedule. They are weak at checking one, especially for problems that only show up across weeks or across files.

A Reddit thread on work hour reporting shows how this goes wrong. Residents described how their hospital's tracking software counted all paid time off (vacation, holidays, sick days) as zero-hour workdays.

If a resident worked three 90-hour weeks in February and then took one week of vacation, the software reported a compliant 67.5-hour average. The program looked fine on paper. The ACGME leaves vacation out of the average, so that resident's real average was 90, and they had just worked dangerously over the cap for three consecutive weeks.

One commenter said their GME office knew about the problem and did "not intend to fix it." Whatever the tracking shows, the consequences of a real violation fall on the program.

Silos Create Blind Spots

Most programs build their call schedule, block schedule, and clinic schedule in separate files. This makes it nearly impossible to detect cross-schedule conflicts: a resident assigned to continuity clinic at 8 AM the morning after a 24-hour call shift, for example. Each individual file may look fine. The combined reality is a violation.

The Averaging System Conceals Pattern Violations

A schedule can be built in good faith and still be non-compliant. A chief resident who carefully checks each rotation in isolation won't necessarily catch the 4-week rolling average problem until after it's already happened.

Institutional Knowledge Walks Out the Door Every July

Chief residents typically serve one-year terms.

The knowledge about why certain call patterns were ruled out, which residents have exceptions, and how the specialty rules were handled lives in someone's head, not in the schedule itself. Every July, the new chief starts from scratch, often spending dozens of hours rebuilding something that was already built the year before.

Why Checking by Hand Misses Pattern Violations

With 20 residents across multiple rotations there are far more ways to arrange a month than anyone can check by hand. You're not finding all the violations; you're finding the visible ones.

So a program can believe it is compliant without a sound basis for that belief.

A Better Approach: Build the Rules In Rather Than Audit Afterwards

The shift is simple to state. Traditional scheduling is a two-step process: build a schedule, then check it for compliance. The problem is that step two, manual auditing, is unreliable at the scale and complexity of residency scheduling.

The alternative is to write every rule down first, the ACGME ones and your own, and build the schedule to all of them at once. The rules then shape the schedule as it is made, instead of being something you hope the review catches. There is still a review at the end; it just has far less to find.

For a program director who has spent years wondering what is lurking in the call schedule, that is not a minor improvement.

Build the Requirements In From the Start

ACGME compliance anxiety is a reasonable response to a high-stakes problem. Duty hour problems land on the Program Director, and usually surface late, because the manual systems most programs rely on aren't equipped to find them.

More careful auditing of the same Excel files will not fix it. What helps is changing the order: write every rule down first and build the schedule to them, so the review at the end is a check rather than a repair job.

None of this requires you to become an expert in GME scheduling software. Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between checking a schedule and building the rules in?

The key difference is prevention versus detection. Traditional software checks a manually built schedule for potential errors, while building the rules in means the schedule is shaped by them from the start. The review afterwards becomes a check rather than a repair job.

Do we have to replace our current scheduling platform like Amion or QGenda?

No. Keeping Amion or QGenda is entirely up to you. We deliver the finished schedule as Excel or Google Sheets, or on a custom live view if that helps, and many programs simply upload it into Amion or QGenda for day to day viewing. Others use the live view, or both.

How do you handle complex subspecialty rules for programs like surgery or anesthesiology?

Subspecialty-specific rules are written down as core rules for each individual program. Whether it’s specific call frequency requirements for neurosurgery, continuity clinic thresholds for family medicine, or unique shift structures in anesthesiology, these are captured during our intake process and treated with the same weight as the core ACGME duty hour limits.

How does the service handle mid-year changes, like a resident leaving or going on leave?

Changes like a leave are handled by rebuilding the rest of the block to the same rules. You tell us what changed and we rebuild the rest of the block with the same rules in place, so the uncovered shifts are spread across the remaining residents rather than landing on whoever is nearest. Redrafts for bigger changes are part of the service.

What is the onboarding process like?

The onboarding process is a structured intake where we collect all of your program's specific requirements, rules, and preferences. There is no software for your team to install or learn. We work with your Program Director, Coordinator, or Chief Resident to gather all inputs, which are then written down as your program's rule set, so the knowledge stays with the program.

How much time does handing the build over save chief residents and program coordinators?

It depends on the program, but the build itself, often weeks of a chief's time each year, comes off their plate. This frees up chief residents and administrative staff to focus on education and program management rather than tedious and error-prone spreadsheet manipulation.

Can this also improve schedule fairness for residents?

Yes, improving fairness is a primary benefit alongside compliance. We build to whatever fairness definition your program uses, spreading weekend calls, holidays and nights as evenly as the rules allow. A study in Neurosurgery found that a residency that changed how its call schedule was built saw residents' perceived schedule fairness rise from 43% to 95%.
